questions.question: Q: What causes the seasons on Earth?

points.text: The Earth's axial tilt of 23.5° relative to its orbital plane. When a hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it receives more direct sunlight and longer days, causing summer. When it tilts away, it receives less direct sunlight and shorter days, causing winter.

questions.question: Q: What happens at the summer solstice?

points.text: The Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N). The northern hemisphere experiences its longest day and highest solar altitude. Occurs around 21 June.

questions.question: Q: Why is it wrong to say seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun?

points.text: Because Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during northern hemisphere winter. If distance caused seasons, the whole Earth would have summer simultaneously, but the hemispheres experience opposite seasons.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between perihelion and aphelion?

points.text: Perihelion is Earth's closest point to the Sun (~147 million km, ~3 January). Aphelion is the farthest point (~152 million km, ~4 July). The difference is about 5 million km due to the orbit's slight eccentricity.
The apparent path of the Sun against the background stars over the course of a year. It passes through the 12 zodiac constellations and is tilted 23.5° to the celestial equator.

questions.question: Q: Explain what happens at an equinox.

points.text: The Sun is directly overhead at the equator, and day and night are approximately equal in length everywhere on Earth. Occurs around 21 March (vernal) and 23 September (autumnal).

questions.question: Q: What is the precession of the equinoxes?

points.text: A slow wobble of Earth's axis over a 26,000-year cycle, caused by gravitational forces from the Sun and Moon. It changes which star marks the north celestial pole and shifts the timing of equinoxes against the zodiac.

questions.question: Q: Why does a higher solar altitude cause warmer temperatures?

points.text: When sunlight strikes the ground at a steeper angle, the same amount of energy is concentrated on a smaller area, and passes through less atmosphere (reducing absorption and scattering). Both effects increase surface heating.
